package_info.why_malicious: The 'everything' package is intentionally crafted to depend on every other public NPM package, resulting in an extreme transitive dependency explosion. This design causes denial of service (DoS) by overwhelming package managers, exhausting disk space, and disrupting build and CI/CD pipelines. Additionally, it traps other packages in the dependency graph, preventing their removal from the registry. The package serves no legitimate purpose and is explicitly intended to troll and disrupt the NPM ecosystem.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the package.json declares dependencies on every public NPM package, causing the package manager to recursively fetch and install millions of packages, resulting in resource exhaustion and denial of service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Declaring dependencies on the entire public NPM registry is an intentional abuse of the dependency system, designed to overwhelm systems and disrupt normal package installation processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages only declare dependencies required for their functionality. This package subverts that expectation by listing every available package, weaponizing the dependency mechanism.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for a package to depend on every public NPM package.
key_indicators: package.json with dependencies on every public NPM package
Dependency list size far exceeding any normal package
Absence of functional code, only dependency declarations

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, each sub-package's package.json declares dependencies on a large chunk of the NPM registry, collectively ensuring that all public packages are included as dependencies, which amplifies the dependency explosion and denial of service effect.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dividing the dependency list across thousands of sub-packages to systematically cover the entire registry is a deliberate strategy to maximize resource exhaustion and disrupt the ecosystem.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Sub-packages are expected to provide modular, functional code. Here, they are used solely to orchestrate a massive, distributed dependency chain.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate package structure involves thousands of sub-packages, each with massive dependency lists, solely to cover the registry.
key_indicators: Thousands of sub-packages with patterned names and large dependency lists
No functional code in sub-packages, only dependency declarations
Systematic coverage of the entire NPM registry via sub-package dependencies

attack_chain.action: User installs the 'everything' package, triggering dependency resolution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Massive recursive installation of all public NPM packages.

attack_chain.action: Sub-packages are installed, each pulling in large chunks of the registry.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exponential growth of the dependency tree, exhausting system resources and causing denial of service.

attack_chain.action: Packages that are depended on by 'everything' and its sub-packages cannot be unpublished, trapping maintainers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Long-term disruption and administrative headaches for package maintainers.

behavioral_signatures: package.json files declaring dependencies on hundreds or thousands of packages
Packages that depend on every public NPM package or systematically cover the registry via sub-packages
Install operations that trigger the download of millions of transitive dependencies
file_indicators: package.json with an abnormally large dependency list (hundreds or thousands of entries)
Sub-packages with patterned names and package.json files containing massive dependency lists
network_indicators: Excessive outbound requests to the NPM registry during install
Unusually high volume of package downloads in a single install operation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose dependency lists include hundreds or thousands of entries, especially those matching the entire public registry. Flag packages and sub-packages with no functional code and only dependency declarations. Alert on install operations that attempt to fetch an abnormally high number of packages or exhibit exponential dependency resolution behavior. Automated systems should also detect patterns of sub-package naming and dependency overlap that indicate systematic registry coverage.
